derivations.claim: Define $S(\theta)=\sum_i\min(\lambda_i,\theta)$ for $0\le\theta\le\max_i\lambda_i$. It is continuous, $S(0)=0$, and $S(\max_i\lambda_i)=\sum_i\lambda_i$. If $0\le\theta_1<\theta_2<\max_i\lambda_i$, some $\lambda_j>\theta_2$, so the $j$-th summand increases strictly and the others do not decrease. Thus for $0<D<\sum_i\lambda_i$, the intermediate-value theorem gives a unique $\theta$ with $S(\theta)=D$.
For $t>0$, $\ln t\le t-1$: if $t\ge1$, integrate $1/u\le1$ on $[1,t]$; if $0<t<1$, use $\ln t=-\int_t^1du/u$ and $1/u\ge1$ on $[t,1]$. Hence $-\ln t+t-1\ge0$.

Fix $0<D<\sum_i\lambda_i$, its $\theta$, and $c=(2\theta\ln2)^{-1}$. If $\lambda_i>\theta$, then for $0<\delta_i\le\lambda_i$, $$\phi_i(\delta_i)-\phi_i(\theta)+c(\delta_i-\theta)=\frac{-\ln(\delta_i/\theta)+\delta_i/\theta-1}{2\ln2}\ge0$$ by step 1.2; the inequality also holds at $\delta_i=0$ because $\phi_i(0)=+\infty$. If $0<\lambda_i\le\theta$, then $\phi_i(\lambda_i)=0$, and for $0<\delta_i\le\lambda_i$, step 1.2 gives $$\phi_i(\delta_i)\ge\frac{1-\delta_i/\lambda_i}{2\ln2}\ge\frac{\lambda_i-\delta_i}{2\theta\ln2}=-c(\delta_i-\lambda_i).$$ It holds at $\delta_i=0$ by the infinite-value convention. A zero eigenvalue has only $\delta_i=0$ and contributes zero. Thus for every feasible coordinate, $\phi_i(\delta_i)\ge\phi_i(\delta_i^*)-c(\delta_i-\delta_i^*)$, with $\delta_i^*=\min(\lambda_i,\theta)$.

Summing the supporting inequalities in step 2.1 and using $\sum_i\delta_i\le D=\sum_i\delta_i^*$ proves $\sum_i\phi_i(\delta_i)\ge\sum_i\phi_i(\delta_i^*)$. The latter sum is exactly $\frac12\sum_i\log_2^+(\lambda_i/\theta)$; the allocation is feasible, so it attains the minimum.

If $D=0$, nonnegativity forces every $\delta_i=0$, giving the two stated cases. If $D\ge\sum_i\lambda_i$, choose $\delta_i=\lambda_i$ for every i; all rates are zero, and no feasible objective can be negative. These cases complete the endpoint and degenerate branches.

Let $p_{XY}$ be a joint probability vector on finite alphabets $\mathcal X\times\mathcal Y$, with marginals $p_X(x):=\sum_y p_{XY}(x,y)$ and $p_Y(y):=\sum_xp_{XY}(x,y)$. The marginals are probability vectors by [[lem-it-finite-marginals-and-conditionals-are-pmfs]]. The joint vector is the outcome-weight function of the canonical finite probability space from [[def-finite-probability-space-and-event]]; its coordinate maps are finite random elements in the sense of [[def-random-element-and-real-random-variable]]. Define mutual information in nats by

$$I(X;Y):=D(p_{XY}\|p_X\otimes p_Y)=\sum_{(x,y):p_{XY}(x,y)>0}p_{XY}(x,y)\ln\frac{p_{XY}(x,y)}{p_X(x)p_Y(y)},$$

where $D$ is the finite KL convention of [[def-qa-35-finite-probability-entropy-and-stochastic-matrices]] and $(p_X\otimes p_Y)(x,y):=p_X(x)p_Y(y)$. Every ratio in the displayed sum is positive and finite: if $p_{XY}(x,y)>0$, then each marginal sum is at least that positive entry. The sum is over finite support, so $I(X;Y)$ is finite. The base-$b$ version replaces $\ln$ by $\log_b$.

For any $b>1$, define each base-$b$ finite information quantity by replacing $\ln$ with $\log_b$ in its defining finite formula. Then

$$H_b(p)=\frac{H(p)}{\ln b},\qquad D_b(p\|q)=\frac{D(p\|q)}{\ln b},$$

where the second equality is in $[0,+\infty]$ and $+\infty/\ln b:=+\infty$. The same conversion holds for finite conditional entropy, mutual information, and conditional mutual information. In particular, values in bits equal nats divided by $\ln2$.

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$ with $n \ge 1$, let $\mathbb{R}^n$ be the set of functions
$n \to \mathbb{R}$ and let $d_2$ be the Euclidean metric on it
([[lem-metrics-on-rn]]). Then:

1. **Closed boxes are compact.** For reals $a_k \le b_k$ $(k < n)$ the box
   $Q = \{\, x \in \mathbb{R}^n : a_k \le x_k \le b_k \text{ for every } k < n \,\}$
   is a compact subset of $(\mathbb{R}^n, d_2)$ ([[def-metric-compactness]]).
2. **Heine-Borel.** A subset $K \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$ is a compact subset of
   $(\mathbb{R}^n, d_2)$ if and only if $K$ is closed in $\mathbb{R}^n$
   ([[def-metric-topology]]) and bounded
   ([[def-metric-bounded-diameter]]).
3. **The real line.** A subset $K \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ is a compact subset of
   $(\mathbb{R}, d_{\mathbb{R}})$, the usual metric $d_{\mathbb{R}}(x,y) = |x-y|$
   ([[lem-real-line-is-a-metric-space]]), if and only if $K$ is closed in
   $\mathbb{R}$ and bounded.

**No choice principle is used.** The bisection below halves one coordinate at a
time and takes the **left** half whenever the left half still fails to be finitely
covered, the right half otherwise: a rule with two outcomes, decided by a
property of the box, not a selection. That is the whole reason the theorem is
available in ZF, while the general "complete and totally bounded implies compact"
([[thm-complete-and-totally-bounded-implies-compact]]) is not.

The hypothesis $n \ge 1$ is inherited from [[lem-metrics-on-rn]], which defines
$\mathbb{R}^n$ and its metrics only there; the last remark below records what
happens at $n = 0$.

Let $(X,d)$ be a nonempty compact metric space ([[def-metric-compactness]],
[[def-metric-space]]) and let $f : X \to \mathbb{R}$ be continuous
([[def-metric-continuity]]), $\mathbb{R}$ carrying its usual metric
$d_{\mathbb{R}}(s,t) = |s-t|$ ([[lem-real-line-is-a-metric-space]]). Then the
image $f[X]$ is bounded above and below ([[def-bounded-set]]), and it has a
maximum and a minimum ([[def-max-min]]): there are points
$x_{\max}, x_{\min} \in X$ with

$$f(x_{\min}) \;\le\; f(x) \;\le\; f(x_{\max}) \qquad \text{for every } x \in X,$$

and then $f(x_{\max}) = \sup f[X]$ and $f(x_{\min}) = \inf f[X]$
([[def-complete-ordered-field]], [[def-infimum]]).

Nonemptiness of $X$ is a hypothesis and not an oversight: for $X = \emptyset$ the
image is empty and has neither a supremum nor a maximum. No choice principle is
used.

derivations.claim: For each $x$, choose a minimizing $\hat x_x$ from the nonempty finite set $\widehat{\mathcal X}$; finite choice is available by successive selection from finitely many nonempty sets. The deterministic channel $W(\hat x\mid x)=\mathbf1_{\{\hat x=\hat x_x\}}$ has expected distortion $D_{\min}$. Conversely, each channel row is a probability vector, so its conditional mean distortion is at least $\min_{\hat x}d(x,\hat x)$; averaging against $p$ shows every channel has distortion at least $D_{\min}$. Thus feasibility is equivalent to $D\ge D_{\min}$.

For a probability vector $q$, set $H(q)=-\sum_i q_i\ln q_i$, with $0\ln0:=0$. The scalar function $-t\ln t$ on $(0,1]$ extends continuously to zero because $\lim_{t\downarrow0}t\ln t=0$; hence entropy is continuous on every finite simplex. Expanding the finite KL sum in [F1] gives $I(X;\widehat X)=H(p)+H(q)-H(p_{X\widehat X})$, where $q(\hat x)=\sum_xp(x)W(\hat x\mid x)$; all terms are continuous functions of the channel coordinates.

Identify all channels with a point in $[0,1]^{|\mathcal X||\widehat{\mathcal X}|}$. The row-sum equalities, nonnegativity inequalities and expected-distortion inequality define a closed set; the cube makes it bounded. When feasible it is nonempty, so [F3] makes it compact.

By [F2], division by the positive constant $\ln2$ preserves continuity. Thus the bit mutual-information objective is continuous on the nonempty compact feasible set in step 2.1; [F4] gives a point where it attains its minimum. This proves attainment.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Assume AC. Let $X,Y$ be random elements with standard-Borel value spaces $(\mathsf X,\mathcal X)$ and $(\mathsf Y,\mathcal Y)$, and let $P_{XY}$, $P_X$, and $P_Y$ be their joint and marginal probability laws. The product law $P_X\otimes P_Y$ exists by [[thm-sigma-finite-product-measure-exists-is-rectangular-and-is-unique]]. Define the mutual information in nats by

$$I_{\mathrm{nat}}(X;Y):=D(P_{XY}\|P_X\otimes P_Y)\in[0,+\infty],$$

where $D$ is the directional Kullback–Leibler divergence of [[def-kullback-leibler-divergence]]. This definition remains meaningful when one or both laws have no Lebesgue density and does not subtract differential entropies that may be infinite.

Assume AC. Define $\gamma(E)=\int_E e^{-x^2/2}/\sqrt{2\pi}\,dx$ for Borel E in $\mathbb R$. By [[lem-normal-density-has-total-mass-one]] and [[thm-indefinite-integral-of-a-nonnegative-function-is-a-measure]], gamma is a probability measure; denote it $N(0,1)$. For $m\in\mathbb R$ and $\sigma\ge0$, define $N(m,\sigma^2)$ as the law of $x\mapsto m+\sigma x$ on $(\mathbb R,\mathcal B,\gamma)$. This affine map is continuous: for $\sigma$>0 choose $\delta$=$\varepsilon$/$\sigma$, and for $\sigma$=0 it is constant. Its inverse images of opens are open, so it is Borel measurable. [[lem-law-of-a-random-element-is-a-probability-measure]] makes its pushforward a probability. When $\sigma$=0, the preimage of E is all of R if m belongs to E and empty otherwise, so $N(m,0)=\delta_m$ in [[def-dirac-measure]].

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let
$U,V \subseteq \mathbb R^n$ be open and let $T : U \to V$ be a
$C^1$ diffeomorphism. For every nonnegative Lebesgue measurable
$f : V \to [0,\infty]$,
$$ \int_V f(y)\,d\lambda_n(y) = \int_U f(T(x))\,|\det DT(x)|\,d\lambda_n(x). $$

Let $P,Q$ be probability measures on the same measurable space
([[def-probability-measure]]). Absolute continuity $P\ll Q$ has the convention
of [[def-absolutely-continuous-with-respect-to-a-positive-measure]]. If
$P\not\ll Q$, define $D(P\|Q)=+\infty$. If $P\ll Q$, assume AC
([[def-axiom-of-choice]]) as in [[def-likelihood-ratio-as-rn-derivative]] and
let $r=dP/dQ$ be a finite-valued nonnegative measurable representative of its
Radon–Nikodym class; such a representative exists by
[[lem-radon-nikodym-density-of-a-finite-positive-measure-has-a-nonnegative-representative]].
On $\{r=0\}$ set $\ell=0$, and on $\{r>0\}$ set $\ell=\log r$. This
function is measurable: for $a\ge0$, $\{\ell>a\}=\{r>\exp(a)\}$, and for
$a<0$, $\{\ell>a\}=\{r=0\}\cup\{r>\exp(a)\}$, by the inverse and
monotonicity properties of the natural logarithm
([[def-natural-logarithm]], [[thm-natural-logarithm-laws]]). These are
measurable sets by [[def-extended-real-valued-measurable-function]]. Since
$P(\{r=0\})=\int_{\{r=0\}}r\,dQ=0$ by
[[thm-likelihood-ratio-change-of-measure]], the value chosen there does not
affect $\int\ell\,dP$. Define
$$D(P\|Q):=\int \ell\,dP,$$
where $\log$ is the natural logarithm ([[def-natural-logarithm]]).

The definition is independent of the representative: two representatives
agree $Q$-almost everywhere, hence $P$-almost everywhere. Put
$$\psi(0):=0,\qquad \psi(t):=t\log t\quad(t>0).$$
The function $\psi$ is continuous at zero: for $s\ge1$,
$$0\le \frac{\log s}{s}=\frac1s\int_1^s\frac{du}{u}\le\frac1s\int_1^s\frac{du}{\sqrt u}\le\frac2{\sqrt s}.$$
Thus $t\log t\to0$ as $t\downarrow0$; here $L=\log$ by
[[cor-integral-logarithm-agrees-with-natural-logarithm]] and
[[def-integral-logarithm]]. On $(0,\infty)$, $\psi$ is a product of continuous
functions by [[thm-natural-logarithm-laws]] and
[[thm-algebra-of-continuous-functions]], so $\psi$ is continuous on
$[0,\infty)$ and $\psi(r)$ is measurable by
[[def-extended-real-valued-measurable-function]]. Its signed integral is
defined by the positive and negative parts
([[def-positive-and-negative-parts-of-a-function]],
[[def-nonnegative-lebesgue-integral]]).

For $0<t\le1$, the function $-t\log t$ has derivative $-\log t-1$ and
maximum $1/e$ at $t=1/e$: $e=\exp(1)>1$ by
[[def-real-exponential-function-and-e]] and
[[thm-exponential-is-strictly-increasing]], $1/e=\exp(-1)$ by
[[cor-exponential-reciprocal-and-positivity]], and $\log(1/e)=-1$ by
[[thm-natural-logarithm-laws]] and the inverse definition. The mean value
theorem gives increase before and decrease after this point
([[thm-algebra-of-derivatives]], [[thm-integral-logarithm-derivative-and-normalisation]],
[[cor-integral-logarithm-agrees-with-natural-logarithm]], [[cor-mean-value-theorem]]).
At $t=0$ the negative part is zero. Since $Q$ is a probability measure,
$$\int \psi(r)^-\,dQ\le\frac1e.$$
The change-of-measure identity of [[thm-likelihood-ratio-change-of-measure]],
applied to $\ell^-$ gives $\int\ell^-\,dP=\int\psi(r)^-\,dQ\le1/e$,
so $\int\ell\,dP$ is well-defined; applying it to both positive and negative
parts gives
$$D(P\|Q)=\int\ell\,dP=\int\psi(r)\,dQ=\int r\log r\,dQ,$$
with $0\log0:=0$ and a finite negative part. Therefore the extended integral
is well-defined without an $\infty-\infty$ ambiguity.

This convention is directional: the first argument must be absolutely
continuous with respect to the second for the integral formula to apply.

Let $E,F$ be standard-Borel spaces, let $\mu,
u$ be probability measures on E, and let $K,L:Eightsquigarrow F$ be probability kernels. Let $P=\mu\ltimes K$ and $Q=
u\ltimes L$ be the joint probability laws defined by
$$P(C)=\int_E K(x,C_x)\,\mu(dx),\qquad Q(C)=\int_E L(x,C_x)\,
u(dx)$$
for product-measurable $C\subseteq E	imes F$. Then
$$D(P\|Q)=D(\mu\|
u)+\int_E D(K(x,\cdot)\|L(x,\cdot))\,\mu(dx)=D(\mu\|
u)+D_\mu(K\|L),$$
as an equality in $[0,+\infty]$. In particular, when $\mu=
u$, the joint KL is the conditional KL from [[def-conditional-kl-for-probability-kernels]].

Assume AC and use the directional convention of
[[def-kullback-leibler-divergence]]. For probability measures $P,Q$ on one
measurable space, $D(P\|Q)\ge0$, and $D(P\|Q)=0$ if and only if $P=Q$.

There is also the following normalized-density identity. Let
$(\mathsf X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a sigma-finite measure space: it is a set
with a sigma-algebra and measure ([[def-measure-space]]), and there is a
countable measurable cover by sets of finite $\mu$-measure
([[def-finite-sigma-finite-and-semifinite-measures]]). Let
$\gamma:\mathsf X\to[0,\infty)$ be a finite-valued measurable function with
$Z:=\int\gamma\,d\mu\in(0,\infty)$, and put $\pi=\gamma/Z$. Let
$q:\mathsf X\to[0,\infty)$ be a finite-valued measurable probability density,
so $\int q\,d\mu=1$, and suppose $q=0$ $\mu$-almost everywhere on
$\{\gamma=0\}$. Assume
$$\int q\bigl(|\log\gamma|+|\log q|\bigr)\,d\mu<\infty,$$
where each term with $q=0$ is defined to be zero. Then
$$\log Z =\int q(\log\gamma-\log q)\,d\mu +D(q\,\mu\|\pi\,\mu).$$
In particular, the first integral is at most $\log Z$. This identity concerns
normalized densities only; it does not assert posterior existence for an
unspecified statistical model.

Assume AC. Let $\lambda$ be a probability on $(E\times T,\mathcal S\otimes\mathcal T)$, where E and T are standard-Borel spaces, and let $\beta(B)=\lambda(E\times B)$ be its second marginal. There is a probability kernel $K:(T,\mathcal T)\to(E,\mathcal S)$ such that

$$\lambda(A\times B)=\int_B K(y,A)\,\beta(dy)\quad(A\in\mathcal S,\ B\in\mathcal T).$$

It is unique as a kernel outside a single measurable $\beta$-null set. For every nonnegative product-measurable $f:E\times T\to[0,\infty]$,

$$\int f(x,y)\,\lambda(d(x,y))=\int_T\left(\int_E f(x,y)K(y,dx)\right)\beta(dy).$$

In particular this applies to the joint law of random elements $(X,Y)$, with $\beta=P_Y$; the direction is the law of X given Y.

Let K be a finite kernel from $(S,\Sigma)$ to $(T,\Tau)$, in particular a probability kernel, or a uniformly sigma-finite kernel with the specified exhaustion of the kernel definition. For every nonnegative $\Sigma\otimes\Tau$-measurable function $f:S\times T\to[0,\infty]$, the function
$$I_f(s)=\int_T f(s,t)\,K(s,dt)$$
is $\Sigma$-measurable, with infinity allowed. For a real product-measurable f, the set $D=\{s:I_{|f|}(s)<\infty\}$ is measurable, and its signed integral on D, extended by zero on $S\setminus D$, is a measurable real function. No assertion here is made for a general kernel lacking a common measurable finite-mass exhaustion.

Let $(\Theta,\mathcal T)$ and $(\mathcal X,\mathcal A)$ be measurable spaces,
let $\pi$ be a probability measure on $(\Theta,\mathcal T)$, and let
$K:\Theta\times\mathcal A\to[0,1]$ be a probability kernel. For
$C\in\mathcal T\otimes\mathcal A$, write
$C_\theta=\{x\in\mathcal X:(\theta,x)\in C\}$ and set
$$J(C)=\int_\Theta K(\theta,C_\theta)\,\pi(d\theta).$$
Then $J$ is a probability measure on the product sigma-algebra, and for every
nonnegative product-measurable $h$,
$$\int_{\Theta\times\mathcal X}h(\theta,x)\,J(d\theta,dx)=\int_\Theta\left(\int_\mathcal Xh(\theta,x)\,K(\theta,dx)\right)\pi(d\theta).$$
In particular, $J(A\times B)=\int_AK(\theta,B)\,\pi(d\theta)$ for
$A\in\mathcal T$ and $B\in\mathcal A$.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B,\nu)$ be sigma-finite measure
spaces. Then:

1. the set function $E \mapsto (\mu \times \nu)(E)$ of
   [[def-product-measure-on-sigma-finite-spaces]] is a measure on
   $\mathcal A \otimes \mathcal B$;
2. for measurable rectangles,
   $$(\mu \times \nu)(A \times B)=\mu(A)\nu(B),$$
   with the nonnegative extended-product convention $0\cdot\infty=\infty\cdot0=0$;
3. the measure $\mu \times \nu$ is sigma-finite; and
4. it is the unique measure on $\mathcal A \otimes \mathcal B$ with the
   rectangle formula.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B,\nu)$ be sigma-finite measure
spaces, and let $f : X \times Y \to [0,\infty]$ be product-measurable. Then
$x \mapsto \int_Y f_x\,d\nu$ and $y \mapsto \int_X f^y\,d\mu$ are measurable,
and

$$\int_{X \times Y} f\,d(\mu \times \nu) = \int_X \left(\int_Y f_x\,d\nu\right)d\mu = \int_Y \left(\int_X f^y\,d\mu\right)d\nu.$$

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be an arbitrary measure space and let $f:X\to[0,+\infty]$ be measurable. Then
$$\int f\,d\mu=0 \qquad\Longleftrightarrow\qquad f=0 \text{ almost everywhere.}$$

Let $\phi:(E,\mathcal E)\to(F,\mathcal F)$ be a measurable bijection with measurable inverse. For probability measures P,Q on E, let $\phi_\#P,\phi_\#Q$ be their push-forwards. Then
$$D(\phi_\#P\|\phi_\#Q)=D(P\|Q).$$

The measurable space $(\mathbb R,\mathcal B(\mathbb R))$ with its usual
topology is standard Borel.

derivations.claim: By [F2]–[F3], $X\sim N(0,\sigma^2)$ has the everywhere-positive density $p_X(x)=(2\pi\sigma^2)^{-1/2}e^{-x^2/(2\sigma^2)}$, and $N(y,D)$ has density $q_y(x)=(2\pi D)^{-1/2}e^{-(x-y)^2/(2D)}$. Let $\gamma=N(0,1)$ and set $L(y,A)=\int \mathbf1_A(y+\sqrt D z)\,\gamma(dz)$ for Borel $A$. The integrand is product-measurable, so [F8] makes $y\mapsto L(y,A)$ measurable; each $L(y,\cdot)=N(y,D)$ is a probability. Thus [F8] gives a joint law $Q$ on the coordinate order $(Y,X)$ with base $P_Y$ and conditional kernel $L$. By [F9], $Q$ and $P_Y\otimes P_X$ have respective densities $q_y(x)$ and $p_X(x)$ relative to $P_Y\otimes\lambda$, so they are equivalent. If $P_{YX}\not\ll P_Y\otimes P_X$, [F1] and [F10] give $I_{\mathrm{nat}}(X;Y)=+\infty$, so the result holds. Otherwise equivalence gives $P_{YX}\ll Q$ as well.

On the remaining case, the logarithm of the reference-density ratio is $$\ln\frac{q_Y(X)}{p_X(X)}=\frac12\ln\frac{\sigma^2}{D}-\frac{(X-Y)^2}{2D}+\frac{X^2}{2\sigma^2}.$$ It is integrable because $\mathbb E(X-Y)^2=\delta<\infty$ and $\mathbb E X^2=\sigma^2$. The Radon–Nikodym chain identity $dP_{YX}/d(P_Y\otimes P_X)=(dP_{YX}/dQ)(dQ/d(P_Y\otimes P_X))$, integrated using [F4] and [F10], gives $$I_{\mathrm{nat}}(X;Y)=D(P_{YX}\|Q)+\frac12\ln\frac{\sigma^2}{D}+\frac12-\frac{\delta}{2D}.$$ The finite cross term prevents an $\infty-\infty$ ambiguity if the first divergence is infinite.

By [F11] the real source and reconstruction spaces are standard Borel, so [F7] supplies a conditional kernel for $X$ given $Y$ under $P_{YX}$. The law $Q$ has the same $Y$-marginal and conditional kernel $N(y,D)$. Thus [F5] expresses $D(P_{YX}\|Q)$ as an integral of conditional KL divergences, which is nonnegative by [F6], including the value $+\infty$. Also $\delta\le D$, so $1/2-\delta/(2D)\ge0$. The identity in step 2.1 gives the claimed lower bound.

A test channel is a stochastic matrix $W(\hat x\mid x)$, and its expected single-letter distortion is $\sum_{x,\hat x}p(x)W(\hat x\mid x)d(x,\hat x)$, with block distortion as in [[def-it-single-letter-distortion-and-block-distortion]]. Put $D_{\min}=\sum_xp(x)\min_{\hat x}d(x,\hat x)$. Define, in bits,
$$
R_{p,d}(D):=\begin{cases}\displaystyle\min_{W:\,\mathbb E d(X,\hat X)\le D} \frac{I(X;\hat X)}{\ln2},&D\ge D_{\min},\\[4pt]+\infty,&D<D_{\min}. \end{cases}
$$
The minimum exists by [[lem-it-finite-rate-distortion-minimum-attained]]. Values are not operational code rates; the finite memoryless coding theorem is a separate claim.

Let $\mathcal X,\widehat{\mathcal X}$ be nonempty finite sets, let $p$ be a probability mass function on $\mathcal X$, and let $d:\mathcal X\times\widehat{\mathcal X}\to[0,\infty)$ be finite-valued. Put
$$
D_{\min}:=\sum_{x\in\mathcal X}p(x)\min_{\hat x\in\widehat{\mathcal X}}d(x,\hat x).
$$
For every $D\ge0$, the feasible stochastic channels $W(\hat x\mid x)$ satisfying $\sum_{x,\hat x}p(x)W(\hat x\mid x)d(x,\hat x)\le D$ form a nonempty set exactly when $D\ge D_{\min}$. Whenever nonempty, mutual information in bits attains its minimum over this set.

Let $(a_i)_{i=1}^n,(b_i)_{i=1}^n$ be finite nonnegative real vectors, with $A=\sum_i a_i$ and $B=\sum_i b_i$. Interpret $\sum_{a_i>0}a_i\ln(a_i/b_i)$ as $+\infty$ if some $a_i>0=b_i$; otherwise zero coordinates contribute $0$. Interpret $A\ln(A/B)$ as $0$ if $A=0$ and as $+\infty$ if $A>0=B$. Then

$$\sum_{a_i>0}a_i\ln\frac{a_i}{b_i}\ge A\ln\frac AB.$$

When $A,B>0$, equality holds exactly when $a_i=(A/B)b_i$ for every $i$. If $A>0=B$, both sides are $+\infty$ and no finite equality characterization is asserted.

Let $p_{XY}$ be a joint probability vector on finite alphabets $\mathcal X\times\mathcal Y$, with marginals $p_X(x):=\sum_y p_{XY}(x,y)$ and $p_Y(y):=\sum_xp_{XY}(x,y)$. The marginals are probability vectors by [[lem-it-finite-marginals-and-conditionals-are-pmfs]]. The joint vector is the outcome-weight function of the canonical finite probability space from [[def-finite-probability-space-and-event]]; its coordinate maps are finite random elements in the sense of [[def-random-element-and-real-random-variable]]. Define mutual information in nats by

$$I(X;Y):=D(p_{XY}\|p_X\otimes p_Y)=\sum_{(x,y):p_{XY}(x,y)>0}p_{XY}(x,y)\ln\frac{p_{XY}(x,y)}{p_X(x)p_Y(y)},$$

where $D$ is the finite KL convention of [[def-qa-35-finite-probability-entropy-and-stochastic-matrices]] and $(p_X\otimes p_Y)(x,y):=p_X(x)p_Y(y)$. Every ratio in the displayed sum is positive and finite: if $p_{XY}(x,y)>0$, then each marginal sum is at least that positive entry. The sum is over finite support, so $I(X;Y)$ is finite. The base-$b$ version replaces $\ln$ by $\log_b$.

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$ with $n \ge 1$, let $\mathbb{R}^n$ be the set of functions
$n \to \mathbb{R}$ and let $d_2$ be the Euclidean metric on it
([[lem-metrics-on-rn]]). Then:

1. **Closed boxes are compact.** For reals $a_k \le b_k$ $(k < n)$ the box
   $Q = \{\, x \in \mathbb{R}^n : a_k \le x_k \le b_k \text{ for every } k < n \,\}$
   is a compact subset of $(\mathbb{R}^n, d_2)$ ([[def-metric-compactness]]).
2. **Heine-Borel.** A subset $K \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$ is a compact subset of
   $(\mathbb{R}^n, d_2)$ if and only if $K$ is closed in $\mathbb{R}^n$
   ([[def-metric-topology]]) and bounded
   ([[def-metric-bounded-diameter]]).
3. **The real line.** A subset $K \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ is a compact subset of
   $(\mathbb{R}, d_{\mathbb{R}})$, the usual metric $d_{\mathbb{R}}(x,y) = |x-y|$
   ([[lem-real-line-is-a-metric-space]]), if and only if $K$ is closed in
   $\mathbb{R}$ and bounded.

**No choice principle is used.** The bisection below halves one coordinate at a
time and takes the **left** half whenever the left half still fails to be finitely
covered, the right half otherwise: a rule with two outcomes, decided by a
property of the box, not a selection. That is the whole reason the theorem is
available in ZF, while the general "complete and totally bounded implies compact"
([[thm-complete-and-totally-bounded-implies-compact]]) is not.

The hypothesis $n \ge 1$ is inherited from [[lem-metrics-on-rn]], which defines
$\mathbb{R}^n$ and its metrics only there; the last remark below records what
happens at $n = 0$.

Since $X=Y\oplus E$, the map $(Y,E)\mapsto X$ is deterministic and bijective in E for each Y, so $H(X|Y)=H(E|Y)$. By [F4], $H(E)-H(E|Y)=I(E;Y)$, and this mutual information is nonnegative by [F3] and [F5]; hence $H(E|Y)\le H(E)=h_2(e)$. If $0\le D\le p_0\le1/2$ and $e\le D$, then $h_2(e)\le h_2(D)$: on $(0,1/2)$, $h_2'(u)=\log_2((1-u)/u)\ge0$, and continuity supplies the endpoints. Suppose $0\le D\le p_0$ and $(p,D)\ne(1/2,1/2)$. Then $1-2D>0$ and $q:=(p-D)/(1-2D)\in[0,1]$: nonnegativity follows from $D\le p$ (since $D\le p_0$), while $q\le1$ is equivalent to $p+D\le1$, which follows from $D\le1-p$. R_{\rm erg}(D):=\inf \limsup_{n\to\infty}\frac{1}{n\ln2} I(X_0^{n-1};\widehat X_0^{n-1}),
$$
where the infimum ranges over jointly stationary ergodic pairs of finite-alphabet processes with the given source marginal and $\mathbb E d(X_0,\widehat X_0)\le D$; an empty infimum is $+\infty$.

A best constant reconstruction has normalized expected distortion $D_{\rm c}$ and zero mutual information for every block. Applying the finite log-sum inequality [F4] to the joint pmf and the product of its marginals, both of total mass one, gives nonnegative mutual information; hence $R_n(D)=0$ for $D\ge D_{\rm c}$. Let $S_i=1$ when its chosen reproduction has positive gap from the pointwise minimum, and let $\alpha=n^{-1}\sum_i\mathbb P(S_i=1)$. The excess above the block minimum is at least $\gamma\sum_i S_i/n$, so $\alpha\le\epsilon/\gamma$.

Let $\mathcal X,\widehat{\mathcal X}$ be nonempty finite alphabets, let $p$ be a pmf on $\mathcal X$, and let $d:\mathcal X\times\widehat{\mathcal X}\to[0,\infty)$ be finite-valued. A test channel is a stochastic matrix $W(\hat x\mid x)$, and its expected single-letter distortion is $\sum_{x,\hat x}p(x)W(\hat x\mid x)d(x,\hat x)$, with block distortion as in [[def-it-single-letter-distortion-and-block-distortion]]. Put $D_{\min}=\sum_xp(x)\min_{\hat x}d(x,\hat x)$. Define, in bits,
$$
R_{p,d}(D):=\begin{cases}\displaystyle\min_{W:\,\mathbb E d(X,\hat X)\le D} \frac{I(X;\hat X)}{\ln2},&D\ge D_{\min},\\[4pt]+\infty,&D<D_{\min}. \end{cases}
$$
The minimum exists by [[lem-it-finite-rate-distortion-minimum-attained]]. Values are not operational code rates; the finite memoryless coding theorem is a separate claim.

Let $X_0,X_1,\ldots$ be a source over a finite nonempty alphabet $\mathcal X$, let $\widehat{\mathcal X}$ be finite nonempty, and let $d:\mathcal X\times\widehat{\mathcal X}\to[0,\infty)$ be finite-valued. For positive integers $n$ and $M_n$, write $[M_n]=\{1,\ldots,M_n\}$. An $n$-block fixed-length code with $M_n$ messages is a deterministic encoder $f_n:\mathcal X^n\to[M_n]$ and decoder $g_n:[M_n]\to\widehat{\mathcal X}^{\,n}$; its reconstruction is $\widehat X^n=g_n(f_n(X^n))$, its block distortion is [[def-it-single-letter-distortion-and-block-distortion]], and its rate is $n^{-1}\log_2M_n$ bits per source symbol.

For each $D\ge0$, define the expected-distortion operational rate $R_{\mathrm{op}}^{\mathrm{avg}}(D)$ as the infimum of $\limsup_n n^{-1}\log_2M_n$ over code sequences satisfying $\limsup_n\mathbb E d_n(X^n,\widehat X^n)\le D$. Define the positive-slack excess-distortion operational rate $R_{\mathrm{op}}^{\mathrm{slack}}(D)$ by the same rate infimum over code sequences satisfying

$$\text{for every }\varepsilon>0,\qquad \mathbb P\!\left(d_n(X^n,\widehat X^n)>D+\varepsilon\right)\longrightarrow0.$$

The infimum of an empty set of admissible code sequences is $+\infty$. The expected and positive-slack excess criteria are separate definitions. An exact-threshold condition $\mathbb P(d_n>D)\to0$ is not part of either definition.

Let $\mathcal X,\widehat{\mathcal X}$ be nonempty finite sets, let $p$ be a probability mass function on $\mathcal X$, and let $d:\mathcal X\times\widehat{\mathcal X}\to[0,\infty)$ be finite-valued. Put
$$
D_{\min}:=\sum_{x\in\mathcal X}p(x)\min_{\hat x\in\widehat{\mathcal X}}d(x,\hat x).
$$
For every $D\ge0$, the feasible stochastic channels $W(\hat x\mid x)$ satisfying $\sum_{x,\hat x}p(x)W(\hat x\mid x)d(x,\hat x)\le D$ form a nonempty set exactly when $D\ge D_{\min}$. Whenever nonempty, mutual information in bits attains its minimum over this set.

Let the source and reproduction alphabets be finite nonempty sets and let the distortion be finite-valued and nonnegative. The finite-alphabet information rate-distortion function $R(D)$ of [[def-it-information-rate-distortion-function]] is finite and nonincreasing on $[D_{\min},\infty)$, convex there, zero for $D\ge D_{\rm c}:=\min_{\hat x}\mathbb E d(X,\hat x)$, and right-continuous at every feasible distortion, including $D_{\min}$.

Let $p_{XY}$ be a joint probability vector on finite alphabets $\mathcal X\times\mathcal Y$, with marginals $p_X(x):=\sum_y p_{XY}(x,y)$ and $p_Y(y):=\sum_xp_{XY}(x,y)$. The marginals are probability vectors by [[lem-it-finite-marginals-and-conditionals-are-pmfs]]. The joint vector is the outcome-weight function of the canonical finite probability space from [[def-finite-probability-space-and-event]]; its coordinate maps are finite random elements in the sense of [[def-random-element-and-real-random-variable]]. Define mutual information in nats by

$$I(X;Y):=D(p_{XY}\|p_X\otimes p_Y)=\sum_{(x,y):p_{XY}(x,y)>0}p_{XY}(x,y)\ln\frac{p_{XY}(x,y)}{p_X(x)p_Y(y)},$$

where $D$ is the finite KL convention of [[def-qa-35-finite-probability-entropy-and-stochastic-matrices]] and $(p_X\otimes p_Y)(x,y):=p_X(x)p_Y(y)$. Every ratio in the displayed sum is positive and finite: if $p_{XY}(x,y)>0$, then each marginal sum is at least that positive entry. The sum is over finite support, so $I(X;Y)$ is finite. The base-$b$ version replaces $\ln$ by $\log_b$.

For finite $X,Y,Z$ with a joint pmf,

$$H(X,Y|Z)=H(X|Z)+H(Y|X,Z),$$

and

$$I(X;Y,Z)=I(X;Z)+I(X;Y|Z).$$

In particular, $I(X;Y)=H(X)-H(X|Y)=H(Y)-H(Y|X)$. All terms are finite.

Let $X,Y,Z$ have a joint pmf on finite alphabets and suppose that, for every $y$ with $p_Y(y)>0$,

$$p_{XZ|y}(x,z)=p_{X|y}(x)p_{Z|y}(z).$$

This is the finite Markov condition $X\to Y\to Z$. Then

$$I(X;Z)\le I(X;Y),$$

with equality if and only if $I(X;Y|Z)=0$, equivalently $X$ and $Y$ are conditionally independent given every positive-mass value of $Z$.

For finite $X,Y,Z$,

$$I(X;Y|Z)=H(X|Z)+H(Y|Z)-H(X,Y|Z)\ge0.$$

Equality holds if and only if, for every $z$ with $p_Z(z)>0$, the conditional joint pmf factors as $p_{XY|z}=p_{X|z}p_{Y|z}$; this is conditional independence given $Z$.

Let $(X_k)_{k\ge1}$ be IID square-integrable real random variables, with $\mu=\mathbb EX_1$ and $\sigma^2=\operatorname{Var}(X_1)$. For $S_n=\sum_{k=1}^nX_k$,
$$\mathbb E|S_n/n-\mu|^2=\sigma^2/n,$$
and $S_n/n\to\mu$ in $L^2$ and in probability. Also $\mathbb P(|S_n/n-\mu|\ge\varepsilon)\le\sigma^2/(n\varepsilon^2)$ for $\varepsilon>0$.

Put $D_n=\mathbb E d_n(X^n,\widehat X^n)$, and let $T$ be uniform on $\{0,\ldots,n-1\}$, independent of all variables; set $(X,Y)=(X_T,\widehat X_T)$. Since the source symbols are iid, $H(X^n)=\sum_iH(X_i)$. By [F5], the chain rule, and conditioning reducing entropy from [F7], $$ I(X^n;\widehat X^n)=\sum_i\bigl[H(X_i)-H(X_i\mid X^{i-1},\widehat X^n)\bigr]\ge\sum_i I(X_i;\widehat X_i). $$ Also $I(X;Y\mid T)=n^{-1}\sum_iI(X_i;\widehat X_i)$, while $I(X;T)=0$; the chain rule and nonnegative conditional information [F7] imply $I(X;Y)\le I(X;Y,T)=I(X;Y\mid T)$. For each source word in the high-probability set of step 2.2, the chance that no codeword belongs to $G_n(x^n)$ is at most $(1-q)^{M_n}\le e^{-M_nq}\le e^{-2^{n\delta}/2}$. Source words outside that set have probability tending to zero, so the expected failure probability of the random codebook tends to zero. Since the codebook alphabet is finite, for each n there is a deterministic realization whose failure probability is at most twice this expectation (and if the expectation is zero, a realization with zero failure exists).

Encode each source word by the first codebook word in its good set; if there is none, use a fixed default reproduction word. Decode the selected codeword. The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Assume AC. Let $\mathcal X,\widehat{\mathcal X}$ be standard-Borel spaces, let $P_X$ be a probability law on $\mathcal X$, and let $d:\mathcal X\times\widehat{\mathcal X}\to[0,+\infty]$ be measurable. A feasible joint law, or coupling, is a probability measure $\pi$ on $\mathcal X\times\widehat{\mathcal X}$ whose $\mathcal X$-marginal is $P_X$. For each distortion budget $D\ge0$, define

$$R_{\mathrm{std}}(D):=\inf_{\substack{\pi_{\mathcal X}=P_X\\ \int d\,d\pi\le D}}\frac{D(\pi\|P_X\otimes\pi_{\widehat{\mathcal X}})}{\ln2}=\inf_{\substack{\pi_{\mathcal X}=P_X\\ \int d\,d\pi\le D}}\frac{I_{\mathrm{nat}}(X;\widehat X)}{\ln2}.$$

The infimum of an empty feasible set is $+\infty$. Values are in bits. This definition makes no general existence or attainment claim and supplies no operational coding theorem for arbitrary standard-Borel alphabets.

Assume AC. Let $X\sim N(0,\sigma^2)$ with $\sigma^2>0$, let $Y$ be any real-valued reconstruction jointly distributed with $X$, and suppose $0<D<\sigma^2$ and $\delta:=\mathbb E(X-Y)^2\le D$. Then

$$I_{\mathrm{nat}}(X;Y)\ge\frac12\ln\frac{\sigma^2}{D}.$$

No density for $Y$, conditional differential entropy, or subtraction of potentially infinite entropies is assumed.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $n\ge1$, let $Z\sim N_n(0,I_n)$ have independent standard-normal coordinates, and let $U\in\mathbb R^{n\times n}$ satisfy $U^TU=I_n$. Then $UZ$ also has independent $N(0,1)$ coordinates. Here $I_n$ is the identity matrix and $U$ is orthogonal.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let
$U,V \subseteq \mathbb R^n$ be open and let $T : U \to V$ be a
$C^1$ diffeomorphism. For every nonnegative Lebesgue measurable
$f : V \to [0,\infty]$,
$$ \int_V f(y)\,d\lambda_n(y) = \int_U f(T(x))\,|\det DT(x)|\,d\lambda_n(x). $$

Assume AC and use the directional convention of
[[def-kullback-leibler-divergence]]. For probability measures $P,Q$ on one
measurable space, $D(P\|Q)\ge0$, and $D(P\|Q)=0$ if and only if $P=Q$.

There is also the following normalized-density identity. Let
$(\mathsf X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a sigma-finite measure space: it is a set
with a sigma-algebra and measure ([[def-measure-space]]), and there is a
countable measurable cover by sets of finite $\mu$-measure
([[def-finite-sigma-finite-and-semifinite-measures]]). Let
$\gamma:\mathsf X\to[0,\infty)$ be a finite-valued measurable function with
$Z:=\int\gamma\,d\mu\in(0,\infty)$, and put $\pi=\gamma/Z$. Let
$q:\mathsf X\to[0,\infty)$ be a finite-valued measurable probability density,
so $\int q\,d\mu=1$, and suppose $q=0$ $\mu$-almost everywhere on
$\{\gamma=0\}$. Assume
$$\int q\bigl(|\log\gamma|+|\log q|\bigr)\,d\mu<\infty,$$
where each term with $q=0$ is defined to be zero. Then
$$\log Z =\int q(\log\gamma-\log q)\,d\mu +D(q\,\mu\|\pi\,\mu).$$
In particular, the first integral is at most $\log Z$. This identity concerns
normalized densities only; it does not assert posterior existence for an
unspecified statistical model.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B,\nu)$ be sigma-finite measure
spaces. Then:

1. the set function $E \mapsto (\mu \times \nu)(E)$ of
   [[def-product-measure-on-sigma-finite-spaces]] is a measure on
   $\mathcal A \otimes \mathcal B$;
2. for measurable rectangles,
   $$(\mu \times \nu)(A \times B)=\mu(A)\nu(B),$$
   with the nonnegative extended-product convention $0\cdot\infty=\infty\cdot0=0$;
3. the measure $\mu \times \nu$ is sigma-finite; and
4. it is the unique measure on $\mathcal A \otimes \mathcal B$ with the
   rectangle formula.

Assume AC. Define $\gamma(E)=\int_E e^{-x^2/2}/\sqrt{2\pi}\,dx$ for Borel E in $\mathbb R$. By [[lem-normal-density-has-total-mass-one]] and [[thm-indefinite-integral-of-a-nonnegative-function-is-a-measure]], gamma is a probability measure; denote it $N(0,1)$. For $m\in\mathbb R$ and $\sigma\ge0$, define $N(m,\sigma^2)$ as the law of $x\mapsto m+\sigma x$ on $(\mathbb R,\mathcal B,\gamma)$. This affine map is continuous: for $\sigma$>0 choose $\delta$=$\varepsilon$/$\sigma$, and for $\sigma$=0 it is constant. Its inverse images of opens are open, so it is Borel measurable. [[lem-law-of-a-random-element-is-a-probability-measure]] makes its pushforward a probability. When $\sigma$=0, the preimage of E is all of R if m belongs to E and empty otherwise, so $N(m,0)=\delta_m$ in [[def-dirac-measure]].

Let $(E_n)_{n\in\mathbb N}$ be a decreasing sequence of measurable sets for a measure $\mu$. If $\mu(E_{n_0})<+\infty$ for some $n_0$, then

$$\mu\left(\bigcap_{n\in\mathbb N}E_n\right)=\inf_{n\in\mathbb N}\mu(E_n).$$

derivations.claim: Suppose $\sigma^2>0$ and $0<D<\sigma^2$. By [F2], every feasible joint law has mutual information in nats at least $\frac12\ln(\sigma^2/D)$; division by $\ln2>0$ and taking the infimum in [F1] gives $R(D)\ge\frac12\log_2(\sigma^2/D)$.
If $\sigma^2>0$ and $D\ge\sigma^2$, the constant reconstruction $Y=0$ has distortion $\sigma^2$ and mutual information zero; [F5] makes zero the minimum, so $R(D)=0$.

Suppose $\sigma^2>0$ and $D=0$. Every feasible coupling satisfies $X=Y$ almost surely because the nonnegative random variable $(X-Y)^2$ has expectation zero. The diagonal $\{(x,y):x=y\}$ has joint probability one. By [F7] the normal density is bounded by $(2\pi\sigma^2)^{-1/2}$, so under the product law, for every $h>0$, the event $|X-Y|\le h$ has probability at most $2h(2\pi\sigma^2)^{-1/2}$. For $h=1/(n+1)$, $n\ge0$, these measurable events decrease to the diagonal; [F8] therefore makes its product probability zero. Thus the joint law is not absolutely continuous with respect to the product of its marginals and its KL, hence its mutual information, is infinite. Every feasible coupling has this value, proving $R(0)=+\infty$.

Put $a=\sqrt{\sigma^2-D}>0$, $b=\sqrt D>0$, and let $U,V$ be independent standard normals. Set $Y=aU$, $X=aU+bV$. The orthogonal matrix $\sigma^{-1}\begin{pmatrix}a&b\\-b&a\end{pmatrix}$ and [F3] show $X\sim N(0,\sigma^2)$; also $\mathbb E(X-Y)^2=b^2=D$. By [F7], $U,V$ have product density; the invertible map $(u,v)\mapsto(x,y)=(au+bv,au)$ has determinant $-ab$, so [F4] gives joint density $(2\pi ab)^{-1}\exp[-y^2/(2a^2)-(x-y)^2/(2b^2)]$. The product of the $N(0,\sigma^2)$ and $N(0,a^2)$ marginals has density $(2\pi\sigma a)^{-1}\exp[-x^2/(2\sigma^2)-y^2/(2a^2)]$. Their log-density ratio has expectation $\ln(\sigma/b)-\frac12+\frac12=\frac12\ln(\sigma^2/D)$; [F1] therefore gives a feasible joint law attaining the lower bound in step 1.1.

If $\sigma^2=0$, then $X=0$ almost surely. The constant reconstruction $Y=0$ has zero distortion and zero mutual information, while [F5] gives a nonnegative lower bound for every feasible coupling. Therefore $R(D)=0$ for every $D\ge0$. These branches prove the statement.

where $D$ is the directional Kullback–Leibler divergence of [[def-kullback-leibler-divergence]]. This definition remains meaningful when one or both laws have no Lebesgue density and does not subtract differential entropies that may be infinite.

Let $(E,\mathcal E)$ and $(F,\mathcal F)$ be measurable spaces and let $P$ be a probability measure on $(E\times F,\mathcal E\otimes\mathcal F)$. Its marginals are $P_E(A)=P(A\times F)$ and $P_F(B)=P(E\times B)$. The product probability $P_E\otimes P_F$ exists by the finite product-measure theorem. For the absolutely continuous branch $P\ll P_E\otimes P_F$, assume AC as required by [[def-kullback-leibler-divergence]]; the non-absolutely-continuous branch below remains $+\infty$. Define the **measure-theoretic mutual information** of the joint law $P$ by
$$I(P):=D(P\|P_E\otimes P_F)\in[0,+\infty].$$
For random elements $X,Y$ with joint law $P_{XY}$, write $I(X;Y):=I(P_{XY})$. The logarithm convention is the natural logarithm, so finite values are in nats as fixed by [[def-it-information-units-and-logarithm-base]]. The divergence is directional in its two law arguments and is $+\infty$ when $P_{XY}\not\ll P_X\otimes P_Y$.

This definition uses only the joint law, not a choice of density or a difference of entropy quantities.

For standard-Borel random elements X,Y,Z,
$$I((Z,X);Y)=I(Z;Y)+I(X;Y\mid Z).$$
The right side is a sum in $[0,+\infty]$. This chain rule is asserted as an equality of extended nonnegative quantities; no difference of possibly infinite entropies or divergences occurs.

Let $\phi:(E,\mathcal E)\to(F,\mathcal F)$ be a measurable bijection with measurable inverse. For probability measures P,Q on E, let $\phi_\#P,\phi_\#Q$ be their push-forwards. Then
$$D(\phi_\#P\|\phi_\#Q)=D(P\|Q).$$

Let $E,F$ be standard-Borel spaces, let $\mu,
u$ be probability measures on E, and let $K,L:Eightsquigarrow F$ be probability kernels. Let $P=\mu\ltimes K$ and $Q=
u\ltimes L$ be the joint probability laws defined by
$$P(C)=\int_E K(x,C_x)\,\mu(dx),\qquad Q(C)=\int_E L(x,C_x)\,
u(dx)$$
for product-measurable $C\subseteq E	imes F$. Then
$$D(P\|Q)=D(\mu\|
u)+\int_E D(K(x,\cdot)\|L(x,\cdot))\,\mu(dx)=D(\mu\|
u)+D_\mu(K\|L),$$
as an equality in $[0,+\infty]$. In particular, when $\mu=
u$, the joint KL is the conditional KL from [[def-conditional-kl-for-probability-kernels]].

Assume AC. Let X,Y,Z be random elements with standard-Borel value spaces and write $P_{ZXY}$ for the joint law of $(Z,X,Y)$ in that coordinate order. Let $K(z,\cdot)$ and $L(z,\cdot)$ be regular conditional laws of X and Y given Z=z. Let R be the probability law on the same product space whose rectangle values are
$$R(C\times A\times B)=\int_C K(z,A)L(z,B)\,P_Z(dz).$$
Its existence, uniqueness, and independence of the versions K,L are established in [[lem-same-marginal-conditional-product-law-well-defined]]. Define the **conditional mutual information** by
$$I(X;Y\mid Z):=D(P_{ZXY}\|R)\in[0,+\infty].$$
The reference R has the same Z marginal as the joint law and makes X,Y independent conditionally on Z. The logarithm is natural, so finite values are measured in nats under [[def-it-information-units-and-logarithm-base]]. The definition is a divergence between full probability laws; it does not subtract two possibly infinite entropies.

Assume AC and use the directional convention of
[[def-kullback-leibler-divergence]]. For probability measures $P,Q$ on one
measurable space, $D(P\|Q)\ge0$, and $D(P\|Q)=0$ if and only if $P=Q$.

There is also the following normalized-density identity. Let
$(\mathsf X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a sigma-finite measure space: it is a set
with a sigma-algebra and measure ([[def-measure-space]]), and there is a
countable measurable cover by sets of finite $\mu$-measure
([[def-finite-sigma-finite-and-semifinite-measures]]). Let
$\gamma:\mathsf X\to[0,\infty)$ be a finite-valued measurable function with
$Z:=\int\gamma\,d\mu\in(0,\infty)$, and put $\pi=\gamma/Z$. Let
$q:\mathsf X\to[0,\infty)$ be a finite-valued measurable probability density,
so $\int q\,d\mu=1$, and suppose $q=0$ $\mu$-almost everywhere on
$\{\gamma=0\}$. Assume
$$\int q\bigl(|\log\gamma|+|\log q|\bigr)\,d\mu<\infty,$$
where each term with $q=0$ is defined to be zero. Then
$$\log Z =\int q(\log\gamma-\log q)\,d\mu +D(q\,\mu\|\pi\,\mu).$$
In particular, the first integral is at most $\log Z$. This identity concerns
normalized densities only; it does not assert posterior existence for an
unspecified statistical model.

Assume AC. Let $X\sim N(0,\sigma^2)$ with $\sigma^2>0$, let $Y$ be any real-valued reconstruction jointly distributed with $X$, and suppose $0<D<\sigma^2$ and $\delta:=\mathbb E(X-Y)^2\le D$. Then

$$I_{\mathrm{nat}}(X;Y)\ge\frac12\ln\frac{\sigma^2}{D}.$$

No density for $Y$, conditional differential entropy, or subtraction of potentially infinite entropies is assumed.

Let $m\ge1$, let $\lambda_1,\ldots,\lambda_m\ge0$, and for $0\le\delta_i\le\lambda_i$ put

$$\phi_i(\delta_i):=\begin{cases}\frac12\log_2(\lambda_i/\delta_i),&\lambda_i>0,\ 0<\delta_i\le\lambda_i,\\+\infty,&\lambda_i>0,\ \delta_i=0,\\0,&\lambda_i=0,\ \delta_i=0.\end{cases}$$

For a total distortion budget $D\ge0$, minimize $\sum_i\phi_i(\delta_i)$ subject to $\sum_i\delta_i\le D$ and $0\le\delta_i\le\lambda_i$. If $0<D<\sum_i\lambda_i$, there is a unique $\theta\in(0,\max_i\lambda_i)$ satisfying

$$\sum_i\min(\lambda_i,\theta)=D,$$

and the minimum is

$$\frac12\sum_i\log_2^+(\lambda_i/\theta),\qquad \delta_i^*=\min(\lambda_i,\theta),$$

where $\log_2^+(u):=\max(0,\log_2 u)$ for $u>0$, and $\log_2^+(0):=0$. If $D=0$, the minimum is $+\infty$ when some $\lambda_i>0$ and is $0$ when all $\lambda_i=0$. If $D\ge\sum_i\lambda_i$, the minimum is $0$.

By [[lem-normal-density-has-total-mass-one]] and [[thm-indefinite-integral-of-a-nonnegative-function-is-a-measure]], gamma is a probability measure; denote it $N(0,1)$. For $m\in\mathbb R$ and $\sigma\ge0$, define $N(m,\sigma^2)$ as the law of $x\mapsto m+\sigma x$ on $(\mathbb R,\mathcal B,\gamma)$. This affine map is continuous: for $\sigma$>0 choose $\delta$=$\varepsilon$/$\sigma$, and for $\sigma$=0 it is constant. Its inverse images of opens are open, so it is Borel measurable. [[lem-law-of-a-random-element-is-a-probability-measure]] makes its pushforward a probability. When $\sigma$=0, the preimage of E is all of R if m belongs to E and empty otherwise, so $N(m,0)=\delta_m$ in [[def-dirac-measure]].

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let
$U,V \subseteq \mathbb R^n$ be open and let $T : U \to V$ be a
$C^1$ diffeomorphism. For every nonnegative Lebesgue measurable
$f : V \to [0,\infty]$,
$$ \int_V f(y)\,d\lambda_n(y) = \int_U f(T(x))\,|\det DT(x)|\,d\lambda_n(x). $$

Let $(E_n)_{n\in\mathbb N}$ be a decreasing sequence of measurable sets for a measure $\mu$. If $\mu(E_{n_0})<+\infty$ for some $n_0$, then

$$\mu\left(\bigcap_{n\in\mathbb N}E_n\right)=\inf_{n\in\mathbb N}\mu(E_n).$$

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $n\ge1$, let $Z\sim N_n(0,I_n)$ have independent standard-normal coordinates, and let $U\in\mathbb R^{n\times n}$ satisfy $U^TU=I_n$. Then $UZ$ also has independent $N(0,1)$ coordinates. Here $I_n$ is the identity matrix and $U$ is orthogonal.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B,\nu)$ be sigma-finite measure
spaces. Then:

1. the set function $E \mapsto (\mu \times \nu)(E)$ of
   [[def-product-measure-on-sigma-finite-spaces]] is a measure on
   $\mathcal A \otimes \mathcal B$;
2. for measurable rectangles,
   $$(\mu \times \nu)(A \times B)=\mu(A)\nu(B),$$
   with the nonnegative extended-product convention $0\cdot\infty=\infty\cdot0=0$;
3. the measure $\mu \times \nu$ is sigma-finite; and
4. it is the unique measure on $\mathcal A \otimes \mathcal B$ with the
   rectangle formula.

For every natural $n\ge1$, let $\mathbb R^n$ be the set of functions
$x:n\to\mathbb R$ with its finite-product topology and Borel sigma-algebra
([[def-product-topology]], [[def-borel-sigma-algebra]]). Then
$(\mathbb R^n,\mathcal B(\mathbb R^n))$ is standard Borel.

derivations.claim: Write $\delta_i=\mathbb E(X_i-Y_i)^2$, so $\sum_i\delta_i\le D$. Repeated use of [F2] expands $I_{\rm nat}(X^m;Y^m)$ as $\sum_i I_{\rm nat}(X_i;Y^m\mid X_1^{i-1})$. Reorder $Y^m$ as $(Y_i,Y_{[m]\setminus\{i\}})$ by the coordinate-bijection invariance in [F2]. Its derived second-argument conditional rule gives $$I_{\rm nat}(X_i;Y^m\mid W_i)=I_{\rm nat}(X_i;Y_i\mid W_i)+I_{\rm nat}(X_i;Y_{[m]\setminus\{i\}}\mid W_i,Y_i)\ge I_{\rm nat}(X_i;Y_i\mid W_i),$$ by nonnegativity [F3]; the empty tuple has zero information.

If $\lambda_i>0$ and $0<\delta_i<\lambda_i$, [F4] gives $I_{\rm nat}(X_i;Y_i)\ge\frac12\ln(\lambda_i/\delta_i)$. If $\delta_i\ge\lambda_i$, nonnegativity gives $I_{\rm nat}(X_i;Y_i)\ge0=\frac12\ln^+(\lambda_i/\delta_i)$; if $\lambda_i=0$, the same zero lower bound holds. Writing $f_i$ for its bounded normal density, the product law assigns probability at most $2h\|f_i\|_\infty$ to $|x_i-y_i|\le h$, for each $h>0$; taking $h=1/n$ and applying [F8] to these decreasing neighborhoods gives product probability zero on the diagonal. The joint law gives the diagonal probability one, so the KL is infinite.

Independence gives $P_{X_iW_i}=P_{X_i}\otimes P_{W_i}$, so $I_{\rm nat}(X_i;W_i)=0$ from the KL definition. The derived second-argument rule in [F2] gives $$I_{\rm nat}(X_i;(W_i,Y_i))=0+I_{\rm nat}(X_i;Y_i\mid W_i)=I_{\rm nat}(X_i;Y_i\mid W_i).$$ A coordinate swap and the other expansion give $$I_{\rm nat}(X_i;(W_i,Y_i))=I_{\rm nat}(X_i;(Y_i,W_i))=I_{\rm nat}(X_i;Y_i)+I_{\rm nat}(X_i;W_i\mid Y_i)\ge I_{\rm nat}(X_i;Y_i).$$ These identities remain valid when an information value is infinite, since only the explicitly zero term is removed and all other terms are nonnegative. Thus $I_{\rm nat}(X^m;Y^m)\ge\sum_i I_{\rm nat}(X_i;Y_i)$.

For each coordinate put $\bar\delta_i=\min(\delta_i,\lambda_i)$ when $\lambda_i>0$, and $\bar\delta_i=0$ when $\lambda_i=0$. Then $\sum_i\bar\delta_i\le D$. step 1.2 and step 2.1 give the lower bound $I_{\rm nat}(X^m;Y^m)\ge\frac12\sum_{i:\lambda_i>0}\max\{0,\ln(\lambda_i/\bar\delta_i)\}$ nats, with the sum interpreted as $+\infty$ if any positive-variance coordinate has $\bar\delta_i=0$. Dividing by $\ln2$ converts this to the corresponding coordinate-rate sum in bits.

If $0<D<\sum_i\lambda_i$, applying [F5] to $(\bar\delta_i)$ minimizes the bit-valued coordinate-rate sum under $\sum_i\bar\delta_i\le D$ and gives the stated water-level lower bound for $I_{\rm nat}(X^m;Y^m)/\ln2$, hence for the rate in [F1]. If $D=0<\sum_i\lambda_i$, some positive-variance coordinate has zero error, so step 1.2 makes the information infinite. If $D\ge\sum_i\lambda_i$, nonnegativity is the lower bound zero; the all-zero variance case has the same lower bound for every $D$.

In the middle case let $\delta_i^*=\min(\lambda_i,\theta)$. For $\lambda_i\le\theta$, choose the constant reconstruction $Y_i=0$. For $\lambda_i>\theta$, put $a_i=\sqrt{\lambda_i-\theta}$, $b=\sqrt\theta$, and take independent standard normals $U_i,V_i$ using the finite product law in [F10]; set $Y_i=a_iU_i$, $X_i=a_iU_i+bV_i$. The orthogonal rotation with first row $(a_i,b)/\sqrt{\lambda_i}$ and [F9] gives the required $N(0,\lambda_i)$ source; the squared error has mean $b^2=\theta$. By [F6], [F7] and the product normal density, the joint density of $(X_i,Y_i)$ is $(2\pi a_ib)^{-1}\exp[-y_i^2/(2a_i^2)-(x_i-y_i)^2/(2b^2)]$; dividing by the product of the source and reconstruction densities gives expected log ratio $\frac12\ln(\lambda_i/\theta)$. Choose all coordinate pairs independently. Their joint and product-marginal laws factor, and the log density ratio is the sum of the coordinate log ratios, each integrable; [F1] therefore makes the vector mutual information the sum $\frac12\sum_{i:\lambda_i>0}\ln^+(\lambda_i/\theta)$ nats. If $D\ge\sum_i\lambda_i$, choose $Y=0$; the error is the total variance and mutual information is zero. If every $\lambda_i=0$, the same constant reconstruction has zero error and zero mutual information for all $D\ge0$. These constructions attain the remaining lower bounds and complete the proof.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Consider a finite nonempty alphabet $\mathcal A$, a probability measure $P$ on $\mathcal A^{\mathbb Z}$, and the left shift $T(x)_j=x_{j+1}$.

The shift is measurable on the product sigma-algebra. Call $P$ stationary when it is measure preserving under this shift, precisely the condition in [[def-measure-preserving-transformation-and-system]].

For a stationary $P$, call the source ergodic when each event $E$ satisfying $T^{-1}E=E$ has $P(E)\in\{0,1\}$; by [[def-ergodic-measure-preserving-system]] this is exactly ergodicity of the probability system.

Let $(X_t)_{t\in\mathbb Z}$ be a stationary source on a finite nonempty alphabet $\mathcal X$, let $\widehat{\mathcal X}$ be finite nonempty, and let $d:\mathcal X\times\widehat{\mathcal X}\to[0,d_{\max}]$ be a bounded finite-valued distortion. For $n\ge1$ and $D\ge0$, define
$$
R_n(D):=\frac{1}{n\ln2}\min_{W_n:\,\mathbb E d_n(X_0^{n-1},\widehat X_0^{n-1})\le D} I(X_0^{n-1};\widehat X_0^{n-1})\quad\text{bits/symbol},
$$
with value $+\infty$ when the constraint is infeasible. The minimum is attained whenever feasible by [[lem-it-finite-rate-distortion-minimum-attained]] applied to the block alphabets. Put
$$
D_{\min}:=\mathbb E\min_{\hat x\in\widehat{\mathcal X}}d(X_0,\hat x),\qquad D_{\rm c}:=\min_{\hat x\in\widehat{\mathcal X}}\mathbb E d(X_0,\hat x),\qquad R_{\rm block}(D):=\inf_{n\ge1}R_n(D).
$$
The stationary-ergodic process information rate-distortion quantity is
$$
R_{\rm erg}(D):=\inf \limsup_{n\to\infty}\frac{1}{n\ln2} I(X_0^{n-1};\widehat X_0^{n-1}),
$$
where the infimum ranges over jointly stationary ergodic pairs of finite-alphabet processes with the given source marginal and $\mathbb E d(X_0,\widehat X_0)\le D$; an empty infimum is $+\infty$.

For a stationary finite-alphabet source and bounded additive distortion as in [[def-it-stationary-finite-block-information-rdf]], the sequence $R_n(D)$ has a limit for every feasible $D$, and
$$
\lim_{n\to\infty}R_n(D)=\inf_{n\ge1}R_n(D)=R_{\rm block}(D).
$$
The function $R_{\rm block}$ is nonincreasing and convex on $[D_{\min},\infty)$, is zero for $D\ge D_{\rm c}$, and is right-continuous at $D_{\min}$. It is infinite for $0\le D<D_{\min}$.

Let $\phi:(E,\mathcal E)\to(F,\mathcal F)$ be a measurable bijection with measurable inverse. For probability measures P,Q on E, let $\phi_\#P,\phi_\#Q$ be their push-forwards. Then
$$D(\phi_\#P\|\phi_\#Q)=D(P\|Q).$$

Let $X,Y,Z$ have a joint pmf on finite alphabets and suppose that, for every $y$ with $p_Y(y)>0$,

$$p_{XZ|y}(x,z)=p_{X|y}(x)p_{Z|y}(z).$$

This is the finite Markov condition $X\to Y\to Z$. Then

$$I(X;Z)\le I(X;Y),$$

with equality if and only if $I(X;Y|Z)=0$, equivalently $X$ and $Y$ are conditionally independent given every positive-mass value of $Z$.

finite-valued real- or complex-valued measurable representative in
$\mathcal L^1(\mu)$.  Then $A_nf$ converges $\mu$-almost everywhere to a
finite-valued integrable function $f^*$ satisfying

$$f^*\circ T=f^*\quad\mu\text{-almost everywhere},\qquad \lVert f^*\rVert_1\leq\lVert f\rVert_1.$$

The a.e. class of $f^*$ depends only on the a.e. class of $f$.  No ergodicity,
finite total measure, completeness, or invertibility is assumed.
Let $I=[0,1]$ with the subspace topology from the usual real topology and with its Borel sigma-algebra. Then $(I,\mathcal B(I))$ is a standard-Borel space ([[def-standard-borel-space]]).

If $S$ is a nonempty at-most-countable set, then $(S,\mathcal P(S))$ is a
standard Borel space.
Every finite product of standard Borel spaces, with its finite product sigma-algebra, is standard Borel.

Assume the full Axiom of Choice. For every sequence
$(A_n)_{n\in\mathbb N}$ of nonempty sets there is a sequence
$(a_n)_{n\in\mathbb N}$ with $a_n\in A_n$ for every $n\in\mathbb N$. Thus the
Axiom of Choice implies the pair-local countable choice principle
$\mathrm{AC}_\omega$
([[def-countable-choice-principle-for-foliation-pair]]).
Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. A countable product of Polish spaces is Polish, and every $G_\delta$ subspace of a Polish space is Polish.
Assuming $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, a countable product of second countable spaces is second countable.

Let $n \ge 1$, **assume the Axiom of Countable Choice**
([[def-countable-choice]]), and let $a_i \le b_i$ be reals for $i<n$. Write

$$R^{\circ} := \{\, x \in \mathbb{R}^n : a_i < x_i < b_i \text{ for every } i<n \,\}, \qquad \overline{R} := [a,b] = \{\, x \in \mathbb{R}^n : a_i \le x_i \le b_i \text{ for every } i<n \,\}$$

([[def-multidimensional-rectangle-and-volume]]). Then $R^{\circ}$ is open and
$\overline{R}$ is closed, so both are Borel and Lebesgue measurable, and **every**
set $R$ with $R^{\circ} \subseteq R \subseteq \overline{R}$ is Lebesgue
measurable with

$$\lambda_n(R) \;=\; \prod_{i<n}(b_i-a_i).$$

In particular this covers the four one-dimensional face conventions in each
coordinate — the open box, the closed box $[a,b]$, the half-open box
$B(a,b) = \prod_{i<n}(a_i,b_i]$ of [[def-half-open-box]], and every mixture of
them, in any combination of coordinates — and it gives measure $0$ to all of them
whenever $a_i = b_i$ for some $i<n$. For a half-open box with infinite
parameters the value is already
$\lambda_n(B) = \operatorname{vol}(B)$ ([[thm-lebesgue-measure-is-a-complete-measure]]).

A **probability measure** on a measurable space $(X,\mathcal A)$ is a measure $\mathbb P$ with $\mathbb P(X)=1$ ([[def-measure]]). The triple $(X,\mathcal A,\mathbb P)$ is a **probability space** ([[def-measure-space]]); $X$ is its sample space and the members of $\mathcal A$ are its events.

Let $(X,\mathcal T)$ be a topological space ([[def-topological-space]]). The
**Borel sigma-algebra of $X$** is the sigma-algebra generated by its open sets:

$$\mathcal B(X):=\sigma_X(\mathcal T).$$

Its members are the **Borel subsets** of $X$. The generated sigma-algebra exists
and is minimal by [[thm-generated-sigma-algebra-exists-and-is-minimal]].

Let $(X,\mathcal A)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B)$ be measurable spaces. Their
**product sigma-algebra** is

$$\mathcal A \otimes \mathcal B := \sigma(\{A \times B : A \in \mathcal A,\ B \in \mathcal B\}),$$

the sigma-algebra on $X \times Y$ generated by the measurable rectangles of
[[def-measurable-rectangle]].

For the empty family, put $\prod_{i<0}X_i:=\{()\}$ and define its **empty
product sigma-algebra** by

$$\bigotimes_{i<0}\mathcal A_i:=\{\varnothing,\{()\}\}.$$

For a nonempty finite family of measurable spaces $(X_i,\mathcal A_i)$ with
$i<n$, the **finite product sigma-algebra** is defined recursively by

$$\bigotimes_{i<1}\mathcal A_i := \mathcal A_0,\qquad \bigotimes_{i<n+1}\mathcal A_i := \left(\bigotimes_{i<n}\mathcal A_i\right)\otimes\mathcal A_n.$$

This recursive definition is the finite base case used later when the library
passes to countable product constructions.

**The product set.** Let $I$ be a set and let $X_i$ be a set for each $i \in I$.
The **product** is

$$\prod_{i \in I} X_i \;:=\; \Big\{\, x : x \text{ is a function with domain } I \text{ and } x(i) \in X_i \text{ for every } i \in I \,\Big\},$$

and we write $x_i := x(i)$, the $i$-th **coordinate** of $x$. Two elements of the
product are equal exactly when they agree at every index, functions being equal
when they have the same domain and the same values. For $j \in I$ the $j$-th
**projection** is

$$\pi_j : \prod_{i \in I} X_i \to X_j, \qquad \pi_j(x) := x_j .$$

**Notation for a finite product.** For $I = n$ a natural number, which is the set
$\{0, 1, \dots, n-1\}$ of its predecessors, an element of $\prod_{k<n} X_k$ is a
function on $n$ and we write it $(x_0, \dots, x_{n-1})$. In particular $I = 2$
gives the **binary product**, written $X \times Y$ for $\prod_{i<2} X_i$ with
$X_0 = X$ and $X_1 = Y$, whose elements are written $(u,v)$ for the function
$0 \mapsto u$, $1 \mapsto v$. This is the only meaning the symbol $X \times Y$
carries on this page.

**Two facts about when the product is nonempty, stated because they are used and
because they cost something.** If some $X_{i_0}$ is empty then the product is
empty, since no function can take a value in $X_{i_0}$. Conversely, suppose every
$X_i$ is nonempty.

- For $I = n$ a natural number, the product is nonempty, and this is a theorem of
  ZF: [[lem-finite-choice]] applied to the function $i \mapsto X_i$ on $n$
  supplies a choice function $g$ for the family of values, and
  $x(i) := g(X_i)$ defines a member of $\prod_{k<n} X_k$.
- For an arbitrary $I$ the assertion "$\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \varnothing$
  whenever every $X_i$ is nonempty" **is** the Axiom of Choice: it is the
  formulation recorded in [[def-axiom-of-choice]], and the choice function of
  [[def-choice-function]] is exactly a point of the product of a family by
  itself. Every use of it below is flagged at the step that spends it.

**The box topology.** Now let each $X_i$ carry a topology $\mathcal{T}_i$
([[def-topological-space]]). Put

$$\mathcal{R} \;:=\; \Big\{\, \prod_{i \in I} U_i \;:\; U_i \in \mathcal{T}_i \text{ for every } i \in I \,\Big\},$$

the family of **boxes**. $\mathcal{R}$ is a basis for a topology
([[thm-basis-criterion]]): it contains $\prod_i X_i$, so it covers the product,
and it is closed under binary intersections, since

$$\Big(\prod_i U_i\Big) \cap \Big(\prod_i V_i\Big) = \prod_i (U_i \cap V_i)$$

and each $U_i \cap V_i$ is open by (T3). The topology it generates is the **box
topology** $\mathcal{T}^{\square}$, and $\mathcal{R}$ is a basis for it
([[def-topology-basis-subbasis]]).

**The product topology.** The **product topology** $\mathcal{T}^{\Pi}$ on
$\prod_i X_i$ is the initial topology of the family of projections
$(\pi_i)_{i \in I}$ ([[def-initial-and-final-topology]]): the topology generated
by the subbasis

$$\mathcal{G} \;:=\; \{\, \pi_i^{-1}[U] : i \in I,\ U \in \mathcal{T}_i \,\}, \qquad \pi_i^{-1}[U] = \prod_{j \in I} W_j \ \text{ with } W_i = U \text{ and } W_j = X_j \text{ for } j \ne i .$$

By [[thm-basis-criterion]] the finite intersections of members of $\mathcal{G}$
form a basis for $\mathcal{T}^{\Pi}$, and those finite intersections are exactly
the boxes with all but finitely many factors unrestricted:

$$\mathcal{R}^{\Pi} \;=\; \Big\{\, \prod_{i \in I} U_i \;:\; U_i \in \mathcal{T}_i \text{ for every } i, \text{ and } U_i = X_i \text{ for all but finitely many } i \,\Big\}.$$

Indeed the intersection of $\pi_{i_1}^{-1}[U_1], \dots, \pi_{i_n}^{-1}[U_n]$ is
the box whose factor at $i$ is the intersection of those $U_m$ with $i_m = i$ and
is $X_i$ when no $i_m$ equals $i$; and the intersection of no members is the
whole product, the box with every factor $X_i$. Conversely a box with
$U_i = X_i$ off a finite set is such an intersection. Members of
$\mathcal{R}^{\Pi}$ are called **basic product-open** sets, and members of
$\mathcal{R}$ **boxes**. So $\mathcal{R}^{\Pi} \subseteq \mathcal{R}$, with
equality when $I$ is a natural number.

**The empty product.** For $I = \varnothing$ there is exactly one function with
domain $\varnothing$, the empty function, so $\prod_{i \in \varnothing} X_i$ is a
one-point set. A one-point set carries exactly one topology, namely
$\{\varnothing, \{\varnothing\}\}$, since a topology must contain the empty set
and the whole set and there is nothing else to contain
([[def-topological-space]]); so the box topology and the product topology agree
there, and both equal the discrete topology and the indiscrete topology
([[def-standard-topologies]]), which coincide on a one-point set. There are no
projections to speak of, and the initial topology of the empty family is indeed
the indiscrete one ([[def-initial-and-final-topology]]).

**Convention.** Unless the box topology is named explicitly, $\prod_i X_i$ always
carries the product topology in this library. That is not a matter of taste: the
product topology is the one with the characteristic property of the next item,
and the box topology has no such property.

A measurable space $(E,\mathcal E)$ is **standard Borel** if there are a Polish space $P$ and a bijection $h:E\to P$ such that $A\in\mathcal E$ exactly when $h[A]$ is Borel in $P$. Thus the measurable structure is part of the datum; no particular compatible Polish topology on $E$ is selected.

Let $n \ge 1$ and **assume the Axiom of Countable Choice**
([[def-countable-choice]]). Then:

1. $\mathcal{L}(\mathbb{R}^n)$ is a sigma-algebra on $\mathbb{R}^n$ and
   $\lambda_n$ is a measure on it ([[def-measure]]);
2. the measure space $(\mathbb{R}^n, \mathcal{L}(\mathbb{R}^n), \lambda_n)$ is
   complete ([[def-complete-measure-space]]), and every $S \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$
   with $\lambda_n^*(S) = 0$ is Lebesgue measurable with $\lambda_n(S) = 0$;
3. every elementary set is Lebesgue measurable and
   $\lambda_n(A) = \mu_0(A)$ for every $A \in \mathcal{E}_n$; in particular
   $\lambda_n(B) = \operatorname{vol}(B)$ for every half-open box $B$,
   $\lambda_n(\varnothing) = 0$ and $\lambda_n(\mathbb{R}^n) = +\infty$.

derivations.claim: By [F2]–[F3], choose $k\ge1$ and a length-$k$ test channel $W_k$ whose expected normalized distortion is at most $D$. Write $I_k:=I_2(X_0^{k-1};\widehat X_0^{k-1})$ bits for this channel and $r_k:=I_k/k$. The choice can be made with $r_k<r$ because $R_{\rm block}(D)=\inf_kR_k(D)<r$ and the finite-block minimum is attained.

Fix $p\in(0,1)$. By [F4], the consistent finite-dimensional product laws of a mutually independent family $(B_t,U_t)_{t\in\mathbb Z}$, with each $B_t\sim\mathrm{Bernoulli}(p)$ and each $U_t$ uniform on $[0,1]$, extend to a probability law $P_M$ on $\Omega_M=(\{0,1\}\times[0,1])^{\mathbb Z}$ with its product sigma-algebra; the marker and seed processes are independent. Let $(\Omega_X,P_X,T)$ be the source shift system and form the independent product extension $(\Omega_X\times\Omega_M, P_X\otimes P_M,T\times S)$, where $S$ is the marker-seed shift. The product measure exists by [F4], and its rectangle formula makes the source independent of both marker and seed processes. Almost surely there are marker times $B_t=1$ arbitrarily far in both directions: for each fixed starting index, the probability of no marker in the next $N$ sites is $(1-p)^N\to0$, and a countable union handles all starting indices. Thus the marker set partitions $\mathbb Z$ into finite segments between consecutive markers.

The product of the source system and the iid marker-seed shift is ergodic. To verify this, take two bounded real-valued rectangle cylinder functions $f_1(X)g_1(B,U)$ and $f_2(X)g_2(B,U)$. For all sufficiently large shifts $n$, the iid-coordinate windows of $g_1$ and $g_2\circ S^n$ are disjoint, so their expectation factors as $\mathbb E g_1\,\mathbb E g_2$. For the source factor, [F7] gives almost-sure convergence of $N^{-1}\sum_{n=0}^{N-1}f_2(T^nX)$ to a finite invariant function $f_2^*$. Ergodicity makes $f_2^*$ constant almost surely: for each rational $a$, the limsup orbit set $\limsup_{n\to\infty}T^{-n}\{f_2^*>a\}$ is strictly invariant and differs from $\{f_2^*>a\}$ by a null set, so it has probability zero or one; the rational level sets then force a constant value. Since $f_2$ is bounded, dominated convergence and preservation of the source law show this constant is $\mathbb E f_2$. Thus the time averages of $f_2$ converge almost surely to $\mathbb E f_2$, and bounded convergence gives $$ \frac1N\sum_{n=0}^{N-1}\mathbb E[f_1(X)f_2(T^nX)]\longrightarrow\mathbb E f_1\,\mathbb E f_2. $$ The Cesàro correlations of the rectangle functions therefore converge to the product of their means. Their finite linear combinations are dense in real product $L^2$: indicators of measurable rectangles form a generating $\pi$-system, and the class of sets whose indicators lie in the $L^2$-closure of their span is a Dynkin class, since increasing unions converge in $L^2$ on a probability space. The $\pi$-$\lambda$ theorem and density of simple functions give the claim. Cauchy–Schwarz and shift invariance extend the correlation limit to every real $L^2$ function. If $A$ is invariant, its indicator has correlation $\mathbb P(A)$ at every shift, while the limit is $\mathbb P(A)^2$; hence $\mathbb P(A)\in\{0,1\}$.

Fix a pointwise minimizer $\hat x_*(x)$ for each source letter. For a segment beginning at marker $s$ and ending just before the next marker $s+L$, divide its first $k\lfloor L/k\rfloor$ sites into consecutive length-$k$ blocks. At each such block start use its seed $U_t$ and the finite inverse-cumulative rule to sample an output block from $W_k(\cdot\mid X_t^{t+k-1})$; on the remaining $L\bmod k<k$ sites, output $\hat x_*(X_t)$. On the shift-invariant null set where markers do not occur arbitrarily far in both directions, define $\widehat X_t=\hat x_*(X_t)$ for every $t$. The resulting map is measurable because each good-segment event is determined by finitely many marker coordinates and each seed selects among finitely many outputs by measurable intervals; it is shift-equivariant because all rules translate with the markers.

The pair $(X,\widehat X)$ is a shift-commuting factor of the ergodic product system from step 1.3, so it is stationary and ergodic: the preimage of a shift-invariant event in the factor is shift-invariant in the product and therefore has probability zero or one. Its source marginal is unchanged because the construction leaves X fixed.

Let $\alpha$ be the probability that coordinate zero lies in a leftover suffix. A segment of length $\ell$ has $\ell\bmod k$ leftover sites. Summing over its possible start and length gives $$ \alpha=p^2\sum_{\ell=1}^{\infty}(\ell\bmod k)(1-p)^{\ell-1}\le(k-1)p^2\sum_{\ell=1}^{\infty}(1-p)^{\ell-1}=(k-1)p. $$ Marker events in this sum specify a cut at the segment start, no intervening marker, and a cut at the end; the leftover site is one of the final $\ell\bmod k$ positions.

The marker process is independent of X. For any length-$n$ window, condition on the markers and sum distortion over all test-channel blocks fully contained in the window; each such block has the stationary length-$k$ source law, so its expected total distortion is at most $kD$. At most two blocks intersect the window without being contained, and their total distortion is bounded by $2k d_{\max}$. Leftover sites have expected distortion $D_{\min}$ each. Divide by $n$, take expectations, and let $n\to\infty$; the boundary contribution vanishes, while stationarity makes the expected mean distortion equal to $\mathbb E d(X_0,\widehat X_0)$ for every n. Since the expected leftover fraction is $\alpha$, this yields $\mathbb E d(X_0,\widehat X_0)\le(1-\alpha)D+\alpha D_{\min}\le D$.

Let E be the independent marker process B, leaving the independent uniform seeds unconditioned. Its value space $\{0,1\}^{\mathbb Z}$ is standard Borel by [F4] and [F8]. Put $U=X_0^{n-1}$ and $V=\widehat X_0^{n-1}$. Independence in step 1.2 gives $P_{UE}=P_U\otimes P_E$, so $I_2(U;E)=D(P_U\otimes P_E\|P_U\otimes P_E)/\ln2=0$. Coordinate-swap invariance and the first-argument chain rule in [F5] now give $$I_2(U;(V,E))=I_2((E,V);U)=I_2(E;U)+I_2(V;U\mid E)=0+I_2(U;V\mid E).$$ Expanding instead in the order $(V,E)$ gives $I_2(U;(V,E))=I_2(U;V)+I_2(U;E\mid V)\ge I_2(U;V)$. Thus $I_2(X_0^{n-1};\widehat X_0^{n-1})\le I_2(X_0^{n-1};\widehat X_0^{n-1}\mid E)$, using only nonnegative extended sums and the explicitly zero independent term. Conditional on E, outputs from distinct test-channel blocks are sampled independently according to $W_k$, and leftover outputs are deterministic. Enlarge the source window to include every source coordinate in a full length-$k$ block intersecting $[0,n-1]$, and enlarge the output to include each such full test-channel block output plus the leftover reconstructions inside the window. The original source and output windows are coordinate projections of these enlarged finite vectors, so [F6], applied conditionally on each marker realization, bounds the original information by the enlarged information. Conditional output entropy is subadditive across block outputs and leftover symbols. Given the enlarged source and E, the block outputs are independent and the leftover symbols are deterministic, so conditional output entropy is the sum of the block conditional entropies. Each length-$k$ block has the stationary source law followed by $W_k$, and hence contributes $I_k$ bits; each leftover symbol contributes at most $\log_2|\widehat{\mathcal X}|$ bits. There are at most $n/k+2$ intersecting channel blocks, and stationarity makes the expected number of leftover sites in the window $n\alpha$. Therefore $$ \frac1n I_2(X_0^{n-1};\widehat X_0^{n-1})\le\left(\frac1k+\frac2n\right)I_k+\alpha\log_2|\widehat{\mathcal X}|. $$

Since $r_k<r$, choose $p>0$ small enough that $(k-1)p\log_2|\widehat{\mathcal X}|<r-r_k$ (if the logarithm is zero, any $p\in(0,1)$ works). Taking $n\to\infty$ in step 4.2 and using step 3.2 yields a limiting upper information rate at most $r_k+(k-1)p\log_2|\widehat{\mathcal X}|<r$. step 3.1 and step 4.1 give the required stationary ergodic pair and distortion bound.
